subject: Chemistry
title: Iron Bends, Steel Holds: Interstitial Compounds and Alloys
summary: Pure iron bends because layers of atoms slide over each other; less than 2 % carbon in the gaps locks the layers and gives hard steel. Interstitial compounds form when small atoms such as H, C or N are trapped in a metal lattice (TiC, Mn₄N, Fe₃H, VH₀.₅₆, TiH₁.₇): non-stoichiometric, very hard, higher melting than the pure metal, still conducting and chemically inert. Alloys form when atoms of similar size (metallic radii within about 15 %, e.g. Fe 126 and Cr 129 pm) are distributed randomly among each other: stainless steel, brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn), hard and often high melting.

notes.title: 13 – Interstitial Compounds and Alloys: How Transition Metals Get Harder

keyPoints: Pure metals bend because **layers of atoms slide**; anything that blocks the sliding makes the metal **harder**.
**Interstitial compounds**: small atoms (**H, C, N**) trapped in the gaps of a metal lattice; **non-stoichiometric** (TiC, Mn₄N, VH₀.₅₆).
They are **very hard**, melt **higher than the pure metal**, still **conduct electricity** and are **chemically inert**.
**Alloys** form when metallic radii are within **about 15 %** (Fe 126, Cr 129 pm): stainless steel, **brass** (Cu–Zn), **bronze** (Cu–Sn).

blocks.p: Metallic radii from NCERT Table 4.2 (Na from Class 11 Ch 10). Alloys form readily within about 15 %.

Steel: less than 2 % carbon in iron. Carbon atoms (small) sit in the gaps between iron atoms and block the layers from sliding, so steel is much harder than pure iron. The same idea with H, C or N in Ti, V or Mn lattices gives the interstitial compounds TiC, VH₀.₅₆ and Mn₄N.
